summary:
STARS UPON YOU. is a public-facing digital observatory that makes real NASA SPHEREx observations easier to explore, investigate and compare over time. Users can navigate an interactive sky map, select a position or enter RA/Dec coordinates, and retrieve SPHEREx data (the DR1 Spectral All-Sky Cube) by HEALPix tile from AWS S3. They can then inspect spectral channels and use comparison and difference-analysis prototypes. Gaia and AllWISE catalogues add context and cross-matching. Five challenge targets are included: Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

For the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, the project turns a billion-object, multi-band dataset into an accessible workflow for finding changes and moving objects. This matters because these investigations usually need specialized tools. Our roadmap adds a Research Journal and Community Missions, so researchers, students and citizen scientists can contribute to real scientific questions together.
details:
What it does and how it works

STARS UPON YOU. is a web-based digital observatory built around real SPHEREx data. A user picks a position on an interactive sky map (Aladin Lite) or enters RA/Dec coordinates. The app finds the matching HEALPix tile (NESTED scheme) and retrieves SPHEREx data from AWS S3. It then parses the FITS files, spectral channels and observation metadata, so the user can explore the 102-channel Spectral All-Sky Cube (0.75–5.0 μm) and the DR1 spectral images and Quick Release 3 data. Users can compare available observations and explore possible differences over time. Gaia and AllWISE catalogues, queried through VizieR, provide context and cross-matching. The demo includes five challenge targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

Benefits and intended impact

SPHEREx observes over a billion objects, but investigating changes in such data normally requires specialized tools. We bring exploration, data inspection and comparison into one connected experience. Researchers, students, educators, citizen scientists and curious people all get an accessible way in. We aim to make astronomical research more approachable, encourage data literacy and connect people around shared scientific questions. Our next steps are:

  • validating the time-based tools
  • adding more datasets
  • a Research Journal for documenting investigations
  • Community Missions for collaborative tasks
  • a Researcher Portal for scientific organizations

Tools and technologies

  • React, TypeScript and Vite for the app
  • AWS S3 for data access
  • Aladin Lite, HEALPix and VizieR for sky navigation, spatial indexing and catalogues
  • ChatGPT and Claude for software development, debugging, architecture and documentation

All scientific measurements and interpretations come from the astronomical data, not from AI-generated claims.

Creativity

Most tools are isolated image viewers or one-task classification experiences. We combine exploration, real-data inspection, comparison and a path to collaboration in a single observatory.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific validity: the difference-analysis and source-tracking modules are labeled as prototypes that need further validation.
  • Accessibility: a non-expert should be able to start from a sky position and reach real data.
  • Transparency: we credit all data sources and open-source tools, and we disclose AI use.
  • Independence: this is an independent project, and NASA SPHEREx data are used as public scientific data sources.
